rows.text:
• 
 Days sales outstanding in accounts receivable (“DSO”) at the end of fiscal year 2015 was 48 days, compared with 44 days at the end of fiscal year 2014 . The increase in our DSO was primarily due to an increase in sales late in the quarter.

attrs.management_says: The increase in DSO (44 to 48 days per MD&A; 53 to 59 days per computed annual) was primarily due to an increase in sales late in the quarter.
attrs.numbers_show: Quarterly signals show receivables outpacing revenue in Q2 (receivables +60.6% vs revenue +41.2%, DSO 41→47 days) and Q4 (receivables +51.6% vs revenue +34.0%, DSO 45→51 days). The 'late quarter' explanation fits Q4 but does not account for Q2's similar pattern.

attrs.management_says: The increase in DSO (to 48 days from 44) was primarily due to an increase in sales late in the quarter (E38).
attrs.numbers_show: DSO rose in Q2 (41→47 days) and Q4 (45→51 days), not only at year-end. Full-year receivables grew 51.6% vs. revenue growth of 35.7% (E25). Quarterly receivables growth exceeded revenue growth in Q1 (+45.0% vs +43.5%), Q2 (+60.6% vs +41.2%), and Q4 (+51.6% vs +34.0%) (E27, E28, E30). The pattern suggests a systemic lengthening of collection periods or channel loading, not merely a year-end timing effect.
attrs.verdict: explanation does not fit the numbers

attrs.management_says: DSO increase from 44 to 48 days was 'primarily due to an increase in sales late in the quarter' (E38).
attrs.numbers_show: Quarter-end DSO jumped in Q2 (41→47 days, receivables +60.6% vs revenue +41.2%) and Q4 (45→51 days, receivables +51.6% vs revenue +34.0%), but was flat in Q1 (39→40) and improved in Q3 (44→43) (E27-E30). The Q2 surge contradicts a pure 'late in the quarter' explanation.
attrs.verdict: explanation does not fit the numbers

attrs.reason: Management attributes DSO increase to 'increase in sales late in the quarter'. Quarterly signals show receivables outpaced revenue in both Q2 (receivables +60.6% vs revenue +41.2%, DSO 41→47) and Q4 (receivables +51.6% vs revenue +34.0%, DSO 45→51). The late-quarter explanation fits Q4 but is not supported by reported numbers for Q2; no intra-quarter shipment data or term changes are disclosed to explain Q2's jump.

rebuttal.innocent_explanation: The Q2 receivables surge reflects a similar late-quarter shipment pattern as Q4, driven by customer budget cycles at calendar year-end and fiscal year-end; quarterly signals show receivables growth outpacing revenue growth in both Q2 (+60.6% vs +41.2%) and Q4 (+51.6% vs +34.0%), consistent with intra-quarter shipment timing that management monitors via daily/weekly sales reports.

attrs.reason: Management attributes the DSO increase to late-quarter sales (E38), but quarterly data show receivables growth exceeded revenue growth in Q1, Q2, and Q4 (E27, E28, E30) and DSO rose in Q2 (41→47) and Q4 (45→51), indicating a systemic lengthening of collection periods not explained by a year-end timing effect alone.

rebuttal.innocent_explanation: The DSO increase reflects a growing share of sales to large OEM and cloud customers who negotiate longer payment terms, amplified by late-quarter shipments tied to microprocessor launch cycles (Intel/AMD/Nvidia) that concentrate revenue in the final weeks of each quarter.

attrs.final_verdict: explanation does not fit the numbers

attrs.reason: Management attributed the year-end DSO increase to a late-quarter sales surge in Q4. Quarterly signals (E30) show Q4 quarter-end DSO jumped from 45 to 51 days, with receivables growing 51.6% versus revenue growth of 34.0%, consistent with a late-quarter sales surge. The Q2 surge (E28) is a separate quarterly effect and does not contradict the primary driver for the annual DSO change.

rebuttal.innocent_explanation: The fiscal year-end DSO increase from 44 to 48 days (E38) is primarily driven by the Q4 quarter-end DSO jump from 45 to 51 days (E30), where receivables grew 51.6% versus revenue growth of 34.0%, consistent with a late-quarter sales surge. The Q2 receivables surge (E28) reflects a separate quarterly timing effect but does not contradict the primary driver for the annual DSO change.
